summary:
Uttar Pradesh stands under India's national framework for transgender persons. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The most trans-visible public space in Uttar Pradesh is institutional rather than underground. At the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj, the world's largest religious gathering, Pavitra Nandagiri, a Mahamandaleshwar of the Kinnar Akhada and one of its highest-ranking monks, led 15 transgender spiritual leaders in the ceremonial bathing on 12 February 2025, the fourth bath of the 45-day fair, marching alongside Naga Sadhus and Aghori. The jurisdiction's trans religious hierarchy is institutionalised, placing a trans visitor inside a recognised order rather than a marginalised one.

That inclusion is contested. A rival leadership instalment drew protests, gurus threatened to boycott the 2037 gathering, and a top-ranking trans monk who objected was physically attacked on 12 February 2025, so festival-week exposure carries a real but episodic risk of confrontation.

Recorded violence against trans people in the state is a single documented fatality. Kajal, 25, of Kanpur, was killed in a home-invasion robbery; her 12-year-old adopted brother also died, and a suspect was later arrested. The killing entered the 2025 Trans Day of Remembrance list through local press reporting by Bhaskar.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented nationally and reaches into Uttar Pradesh. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, and the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender; transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024; and at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

Exposure for a visitor concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences were removed when the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code. Set against that, the courts remain the strongest protection machinery, with the Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issuing sweeping guidelines on police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

The March 2026 amendment narrows recognition nationally, which bears on what documents and identity claims a trans visitor can rely on in Uttar Pradesh: a self-declared gender identity outside the hijra, kinner or intersex categories may not be legally recognised, with consequences for welfare access and for how officials read an applicant's papers.

The 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence. Trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code, a change that applies in Uttar Pradesh as elsewhere in India.

High courts have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people. The Madras High Court's 2021 S. Sushma guidelines cover police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, and the Allahabad High Court, the high court for Uttar Pradesh, ordered relief for a trans passport applicant in February 2026 after authorities required a medical examination.

The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 assesses police abuse of LGBT+ people in India as limited, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, which sets a ceiling on the general expectation of official hostility while leaving checkpoint encounters as the documented pressure point.
localsOnly:
State governments must constitute Transgender Welfare Boards under section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2020. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment reminded all state governments on 9 October 2020 to act, and issued a further press release on 8 December 2021. Uttar Pradesh has a constituted welfare board, though the sources show no visitor-facing enforcement mechanism attached to it.

Residents' access to welfare schemes is governed by the March 2026 amendment's recognition criteria, which the government presents as widening access to schemes and protection from trafficking while restricting legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex individuals.

The Kinnar Akhada's trans monastic order gives residents of the state a recognised religious standing, with ranks such as Mahamandaleshwar held by trans leaders, though the succession dispute around that order has produced protests and threats to boycott the 2037 gathering.

Local press, including Bhaskar, is the channel through which a trans killing in Kanpur reached the national Trans Day of Remembrance record, indicating that state-level incidents are logged only when local reporting picks them up.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Uttar Pradesh has actually constituted its Transgender Welfare Board, and when, is not sourced here; the inventory establishes only the national requirement under section 10(1) of the 2020 Rules and the central reminders of October 2020 and December 2021.

No source in the inventory records how the March 2026 amendment has been implemented or enforced in Uttar Pradesh, including whether state officials have begun applying the narrowed recognition criteria to identity documents or welfare applications.

Police conduct specific to Uttar Pradesh is unresolved: the checkpoint and custody incidents cited here come from Kolkata, Assam and Chennai, and no Uttar Pradesh-specific record of police treatment of trans people is available in the inventory beyond the Allahabad High Court's February 2026 passport ruling.

The scale of violence against trans people in the state cannot be assessed from a single fatality. The Kanpur killing is the only recorded death in the inventory, and whether other incidents went unlogged is not sourced.

The contested leadership of the Kinnar Akhada, the protests, the reported threats to boycott the 2037 Maha Kumbh and the attack on the objecting trans monk rest on a single report of 18 February 2025 and are not independently corroborated here.
